title: Growth Loops, Not Funnels: A Product Manager's Reframe
excerpt: Funnels leak. Loops compound. Why the most resilient growth strategies abandon the linear pipeline in favor of self-reinforcing systems.
content:
The funnel is the most dangerous metaphor in product management. It's elegant, intuitive, and quietly wrong about how growth actually works.

A funnel implies a one-way trip: awareness → interest → conversion → done. Users enter at the top, pass through stages, and either convert or fall out. The job, the metaphor suggests, is to widen the top and patch the leaks.

But real growth doesn't work like that. Real growth compounds. One user brings another. A feature creates data that improves the product, which brings more users, which creates more data. The output of one cycle becomes the input of the next.

What a Loop Actually Looks Like

A growth loop is any system where the output feeds back into the input. The classic example is a collaboration tool: one user invites a teammate, the teammate experiences value and invites their own teammates, and so on. Each new user is both the result of the loop and the engine of the next iteration.

Contrast this with a funnel. In a funnel, you spend a dollar on acquisition and get a customer. In a loop, you spend a dollar on acquisition and get a customer who brings more customers. The math is fundamentally different.

How to Find Your Loops

Start by mapping how your current users actually discover and share your product. Ask three questions:

  1. Where do new users come from today? Not where you think they come from — where the data says they come from.
  2. What action correlates with a user inviting others? Is it completing onboarding? Hitting a usage threshold? Receiving their first piece of value?
  3. What's the conversion rate on that invitation? If 100 users invite someone and 5 accept, your loop has a 5% compounding rate. That's your growth engine.

The loop you're looking for is the one where step three is highest. Double down there.

The PM's Job: Design the Loop, Don't Just Feed the Funnel

Most PMs spend their time optimizing funnel stages — improving onboarding conversion, reducing churn at month one, A/B testing pricing pages. These aren't bad things to do. But they're local optima.

The higher-leverage work is designing the loop itself:

  • Make sharing a natural outcome of value, not a separate action. The best loops are invisible — users don't think "I'm referring someone," they think "I need my teammate to see this."
  • Reduce time-to-loop. How quickly does a new user reach the moment where they'd naturally invite someone? Every day you shatter off that timeline is a compounding day gained.
  • Measure loop efficiency, not just funnel conversion. Track invitations sent per active user, acceptance rate, and time-to-second-invitation. These are your compounding metrics.

A Word of Caution

Loops aren't magic. They require real value at the center. A loop built on a mediocre product just accelerates the rate at which people discover it's mediocre. Get the value right first. Then build the loop to spread it.

Funnels leak. Loops compound. Start designing for compounding.

title: Finding Your North Star: One Metric That Actually Matters
excerpt: Most teams drown in dashboards. The best ones align around a single measure of customer value. Here's how to find yours.
content:
I once joined a team that tracked 47 KPIs. Forty-seven. Every Monday, the leadership meeting was a parade of dashboards — DAU, MAU, session duration, NPS, churn rate, expansion revenue, CAC, LTV, activation rate, time-to-value, and thirty-seven more.

The problem wasn't that these metrics were wrong. Most of them were useful signals. The problem was that when everything is the priority, nothing is. Teams optimized for whatever metric was mentioned in the last meeting, then pivoted when a different metric took the spotlight.

What this team needed — what most teams need — was a North Star.

What a North Star Is (and Isn't)

A North Star is a single metric that captures the core value your product delivers to customers. It's not a financial metric (revenue, profit). It's not a vanity metric (downloads, signups). It's a measure of customer value delivered that, when it grows, tends to pull financial results along with it.

Think of it this way: if you could only move one number, which one would you choose? The answer is your North Star candidate.

Some examples:

  • Spotify: Time spent listening
  • Airbnb: Nights booked
  • Slack: Messages sent (within an organization)
  • Zoom: Meeting minutes

Notice the pattern: each measures the moment a customer actually experienced value from the product.

The Framework: How to Find Yours

Finding your North Star is a three-step process:

1. Define your product's core value

Complete this sentence: "Our product helps customers _____." The verb matters. If you can't fill in the blank clearly, you don't have a North Star problem — you have a product clarity problem. Solve that first.

2. Identify the moment of value delivery

When does a customer actually experience that core value? Not when they sign up. Not when they pay. When they experience it. For a project management tool, it might be "completing a task." For a marketplace, it might be "a successful transaction."

3. Make it measurable and directional

Your North Star should be a count (not a ratio), measured per relevant unit (per customer, per team), and trending upward when you're delivering more value. "Weekly active teams who complete 5+ tasks" is better than "task completion rate."

The Hard Part: Saying No

The real value of a North Star isn't the metric you choose — it's the metrics you don't choose. Every team has a list of things that matter. The North Star forces you to rank that list.

When a stakeholder asks "but what about measuring X?", the answer isn't "we don't care about X." It's "X is a supporting metric. We'll watch it, but we won't let it override the North Star."

That discipline — holding the line on what matters most — is the entire point.

Start Small

You don't need to get it perfect on day one. Pick a candidate, align the team around it, and commit to revisiting it quarterly. The North Star should evolve as your product does.

But start. One metric. One direction. One team pulling together.

title: Shipping Is a Skill, Not a Phase
excerpt: The gap between a good idea and a live feature is where most PMs stall. A practical framework for getting from spec to shipped.
content:
There's a quiet crisis in product management: PMs who can write a brilliant spec but can't get a feature shipped. They research, they strategize, they produce beautiful documents — and then the feature dies in the gap between "approved" and "live."

I've been that PM. And I've learned, slowly and painfully, that shipping is not the last step of the process. It's a skill unto itself — one that can be practiced, improved, and systematized.

Why Shipping Is Hard

Shipping is hard because it requires a different cognitive mode than strategy. Strategy is expansive — you're exploring possibilities, considering trade-offs, imagining futures. Shipping is reductive — you're cutting scope, making irreversible decisions, and accepting that the thing you're releasing is not the thing you imagined.

Most PMs are better at the first mode than the second. Our training rewards exploration. Our tools (PRDs, strategy docs, opportunity assessments) are built for thinking, not doing. And so we over-invest in planning and under-invest in the messy work of getting something out the door.

The Shipping Framework

Here's the framework I use to close the gap between spec and shipped. It has four steps:

1. Define "Done" Before You Start

Before a single line of code is written, answer this question: What does "shipped" actually look like? Not "feature complete." Not "all the things in the spec." The minimum version that delivers real value to real users.

Write it down. Make it specific. "Users can export their data as a CSV" is a definition of done. "Build the export feature" is not.

2. Cut Scope Ruthlessly

Here's a rule I live by: cut your scope in half, then cut it again. Whatever you think is the minimum viable version of your feature — it's still too big.

The reason is simple: the second half of any feature takes twice as long as the first half and delivers half the value. The polish, the edge cases, the error states, the loading skeletons — they matter, but they matter after the core value is live.

Ship the 80% version. Learn from real usage. Then decide if the remaining 20% is worth building.

3. Make the Work Visible

Shipping stalls when work is invisible. A feature that's "90% done" for three weeks is a feature that's stuck — and you can't unstick what you can't see.

Break the remaining work into tasks that can be completed in a day or two. Put them on a board. Move them across daily. The act of making work visible creates momentum — and exposes the hidden blockers that are actually causing the delay.

4. Set a Ship Date (and Defend It)

Without a date, work expands to fill the available time. This is Parkinson's Law, and it will kill your features.

Set a ship date that feels slightly uncomfortable. Then defend it by cutting scope — not by adding people, not by asking for more time, not by working weekends. Cut scope. Ship what you have. Call it a beta if the name helps.

The Mindset Shift

The most important thing about shipping is the mindset: done is better than perfect, and shipped is better than done.

A shipped feature teaches you things no amount of planning can. You learn what users actually do (not what they say they'll do). You learn what breaks at scale. You learn what matters and what doesn't.

Every feature I've shipped has taught me something I didn't expect. Every feature I've polished in perpetuity has taught me nothing.

Start Your Shipping Practice

If you want to get better at shipping, treat it like any other skill: practice deliberately. Pick a small feature. Set a two-week deadline. Cut the scope in half. Ship it. Reflect on what you learned. Repeat.

The gap between a good idea and a live feature is where product managers earn their salary. Close it.

title: The Problem with Prioritization Matrices
excerpt: RICE, ICE, WSJF, Kano — the frameworks are everywhere. But most teams use them to defer hard conversations, not make better decisions.
content:
If you have attended a product management meetup in the last five years, you have seen the slide. A 2x2 grid. Value on one axis, effort on the other. Dots scattered across quadrants. The presenter says something like "this is how we prioritize" and the room nods.

It feels rigorous. It looks data-driven. It is almost always doing less work than it pretends to.

Why Prioritization Matrices Feel Safe

A matrix gives a team the sensation of having thought through its choices. You have scored each initiative. You have plotted them. You have a visual that says "we did the work." For engineering teams under pressure to justify what they are building, that visual is a shield — it transforms a judgment call into a process output.

The problem is that the inputs to the matrix are almost never as objective as the output suggests.

The Scoring Trap

Take RICE: Reach, Impact, Confidence, Effort. Each initiative gets a score, and the highest scores rise to the top. Clean, right?

The catch is in the word Confidence. It is the escape hatch teams use when they do not actually know what they are scoring. A feature with vague impact gets a low confidence multiplier. A feature the team is excited about gets a high one. The matrix has not resolved uncertainty — it has just buried it inside a formula and called the result a number.

And the numbers are almost always relative, even when presented as absolute. "Impact: 3 out of 5" means whatever the person holding the scoring rubric wants it to mean. Two PMs at the same company will score the same initiative differently because they weight customer requests, strategic alignment, and engineering opinion differently. The matrix makes disagreement invisible.

What Matrices Are Good At

None of this means matrices are useless. They are genuinely helpful for:

  • Surface-level sequencing — if you have ten items that are all roughly comparable and you need a starting point for discussion, a matrix gives you a defensible first draft.
  • Spotting imbalances — a grid can reveal that everything is "high effort, low value" or that the team has no stretch bets at all. That pattern is worth a conversation.
  • Aligning vocabulary — when a team agrees that "effort" means "engineering weeks including QA," the matrix becomes a shared language instead of a each-person-uses-their-own-definition mess.

These are real benefits. But they are conversation starters, not decision engines.

What They Hide

The work a matrix cannot capture is the work that actually decides outcomes:

  • Dependencies — a low-score item that unblocks three higher-score items is not low-priority. The matrix has no place for this unless you add another layer of scoring, at which point you are scoring the scoring.
  • Strategic forcing functions — sometimes you build something not because the ROI is obvious today but because it opens a door that closes otherwise. A matrix scores the door, not the fact that it locks forever at the end of the quarter.
  • Customer trust — a promised feature that five major customers are waiting on may score low on reach and impact today and still need to move up. Matrices are bad at urgency that comes from relationships, not metrics.
  • Opportunity cost of delay — doing nothing also has a cost, and most matrices treat the status quo as a neutral baseline instead of a decaying asset.

A Better Use

The healthiest teams I have worked with treat prioritization matrices as artifacts of the conversation, not substitutes for it. They use the grid in the room, on a whiteboard, with the people who will do the work. They argue about the scores. They change them when someone raises a dependency nobody had named. The final plot is not a verdict — it is a summary of a discussion that already happened.

The unhealthy version is the one that ships to a slide deck, gets forwarded to a stakeholder who was not in the room, and becomes the justification for a decision nobody is allowed to revisit.

Matrices are not the problem. The problem is using them to avoid the thing they cannot do: weigh judgment, context, and timing against each other when the numbers do not tell the whole story.

If your prioritization framework would still give you the same answer in the dark, with no grid in front of you, it is probably adding value. If it would not, you are not prioritizing — you are formatting.
author: Akshar Jothi

title: The Art of Saying No: How Great PMs Protect Focus Without Burning Bridges
excerpt: Every new request sounds important in the moment. The PM skill that separates good from great is knowing which ones to decline — and how to do it without damaging trust.
content:
Every PM knows the feeling: a stakeholder halfway across the org drops "just a small feature" into your lap, and somehow it ends up on your roadmap by Friday. The problem isn't that you agree to things — it's that you agree to the wrong things, and then spend the next three sprints defending a decision that should have been a conversation.

Saying no isn't about being difficult. It's about protecting the one resource every product team has in limited supply: focus. Here's how to do it without becoming the person nobody wants to talk to.

Why "Yes" Is the Default Trap

Most PMs default to yes for understandable reasons. You want to be helpful. You don't want to disappoint someone who took the time to bring you an idea. You worry that saying no means you're not strategic — that you're the person who shoots down everything and ends up with nothing to build.

But every yes has a hidden cost: it delays something else. The question isn't whether the request is valid. It's whether it's more valuable than what you're already committed to — and whether you've made that tradeoff visible.

The Three Types of "No"

Not all nos are the same. The way you decline should match what you're actually declining.

1. Not now — the prioritization no

The request is good, but it doesn't belong on this roadmap at this time. This is the most common no, and the easiest to deliver well:

  • Anchor to existing priorities. "We're focused on reducing checkout friction this quarter — this would pull us in a different direction."
  • Offer a timeline, not a maybe. "If it's still a priority after Q2, let's revisit in planning." Not "we'll see."
  • Capture it formally. Put it in the backlog or idea bank. People accept a no when they see their idea is safe, not discarded.

2. Not us — the strategy no

The request solves a real problem, but not the problem this product is built to solve. These nos are harder because the other person is right about the problem — just wrong about the product:

  • Name the boundary. "That's a real user pain, but it's outside what we're solving for this persona."
  • Redirect, don't reject. "Our adjacent team owns that space — let me connect you." This turns a no into a bridge.
  • Check yourself first. Sometimes a request that seems off-strategy is a leading indicator of a strategy that's drifting. The right no includes the humility to reconsider.

3. Not like this — the scope no

The idea is directionally right, but the proposed implementation would create more problems than it solves. This is where experienced PMs earn their keep:

  • Separate the need from the solution. "I hear that reporting is painful. Can we talk about what specifically breaks?" The original ask might be "add an export button," but the real need is "I can't share results with my manager."
  • Propose the smaller thing that resolves the real need. Often the minimal fix is a fraction of the requested feature and solves the actual problem.
  • Show the downstream cost. "If we add this, we need to support it in mobile, in the API, in the docs, and in QA — forever. Is that the right tradeoff?" Make the cost visible before the decision is made.

When You Should Say Yes to Something That Seems Like a No

Saying no well doesn't mean saying no automatically. Some requests that trigger a "this doesn't fit" reaction are worth a deeper look:

  • Requests that come from multiple unrelated sources. One person asking for X is an opinion. Five people from different teams asking for X is a signal worth investigating — even if the request as stated is wrong.
  • Requests that expose a real gap in what the product promises. If your product marketing says "works out of the box" and users are hitting a setup wall, the fix isn't a feature — it's integrity. Say yes to closing the gap, even if the specific request is off.
  • Requests from people who've been right before. Past judgment is data about whose instincts to trust. Weight the source, not just the ask.

How to Make the No Land

The mechanics of saying no matter as much as the reasoning. A wrong no delivered poorly burns trust. A right no delivered poorly burns trust.

  • Lead with what you heard, not what you're rejecting. "I understand you need the dashboard to load in under two seconds for the executive review" is better than "We can't optimize that." The first proves you listened; the second starts a fight.
  • Give the reason before the decision. "We have 3 engineering weeks this sprint and we've committed to the payment flow work that 4 teams are waiting on. That means we can't take on the new search facet this cycle." The reason makes the no legible; without it, it's a power move.
  • Don't leave a vacuum. A no without a next step feels like a door slammed. Add what comes next: "Let's revisit in the December planning session," or "Try this workaround for now and tell me if it resolves it."
  • Follow through on what you committed to. If you said you'd capture the idea or revisit in planning, do it. Nothing destroys credibility faster than a no that turns out to have been a "no for now" that nobody remembered.

The Outcome Good Nos Produce

The PMs who say no well end up with something counterintuitive: more trust, not less. People learn that when they bring you an idea, you'll engage with it seriously — even if the answer is no. They stop wasting energy on ideas that will die an unofficial death and start bringing you the ideas worth fighting for.

That's the real function of saying no: it raises the quality of what gets proposed to you. The team stops padding the backlog with safe ideas and starts doing the work to find the ideas that matter. Saying no isn't refusal. It's a filter — and the people who learn to use it well get to build better products.
